entries.title: With uncertainty at cornerback, Bears need Jaylon Johnson to give them stability now more than ever
entries.summary: <p>Quietly, deep in the shadows of Madden covers, pass-rush fretting and splashy newcomers, cornerback Jaylon Johnson is one of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a>’ absolute most important pieces for the upcoming season.</p><p>Hardly anyone thinks of Johnson when analyzing the Bears’ concerns and it’s easy to forget about a player whose best talent is subtly making opposing wide receivers disappear. But as he works back from a core-muscle injury that wrecked nearly all of last season, the Bears are depending on Johnson more than they have in years.</p><p>For a defense with a lot to prove, and with Johnson the second-most expensive player on the roster at a salary-cap hit of $24.5 million, they desperately need him to be the lockdown corner he was before the injury.</p><p>“He's a vital part of what we want to do,” coach Ben Johnson said before minicamp practice Wednesday. “You know he's been a Pro Bowl-caliber player in the past, and hopefully we can get that out of him again this year.”</p><p>Last season was so stilted for Jaylon Johnson that his coach wasn’t able to get much of a read on him. He missed training camp because of a leg injury, suffered the core-muscle injury his first game back, missed more than two months rehabbing from surgery, then returned as a limited version of himself for the homestretch and playoffs.</p><p>Johnson hasn’t talked to reporters since the end of the season, and the Bears haven’t made him available this week, but he’s been speaking up with big plays on the field, including a two-interception practice Tuesday, and his coach said culture-wise, “He’s doing everything that we ask of him, so I’m very pleased with where he’s at.”</p><p>Jaylon Johnson has been unpredictable in his seven seasons with the Bears — How many star players demand a trade, as he did in 2023, then mend fences and sign a landmark contract extension five months later? — but everything seems solid at the moment.</p><p>He was a Pro Bowl selection each of the previous two seasons. And he’s still just 27. It only feels like he’s been around forever because of the tumult he’s endured at Halas Hall in such a short time: two general managers, three head coaches, four defensive coordinators. If healthy, there’s little doubt he’ll be the same player he always was.</p><p>His contract could become an issue with two years left on his deal, but there’s no smoke on that front at the moment, and Johnson was in town for some of the voluntary Organized Team Activities early this month.</p><p>“I’m looking for him to be a good teammate, good, strong work ethic, prepared,” Ben Johnson said. “He’s done that when he’s been [here] this spring. That will carry over to training camp as well.”</p><p>All of that is promising as the Bears try to solidify a crucial position.</p><p>The last time they were this reliant on him was 2021, his second season, when he was virtually all they had at corner. That unit went from a debilitating weakness to a strength and now to a major question mark.</p><p>The Bears believed they were set, and then some, at cornerback for the long haul with Johnson and former second-round picks Tyrique Stephenson and Kyler Gordon (both 26) in place. They also have had quality backups, including current corner Terell Smith.</p><p>But there’s a never-ending question about Stephenson’s reliability, and Gordon hasn’t been able to stay healthy lately.</p><p>Stephenson hurt his foot or ankle in practice Tuesday, but was back Wednesday. He’s the top candidate to start outside opposite Johnson, for now, but will battle Smith and others to hold his spot. The Bears also drafted cornerback Malik Muhammad in the fourth round out of Texas this year, handpicked to fit defensive coordinator Dennis Allen’s ideals.</p><p>Gordon, a nickel cornerback who missed 14 games because of three separate injuries last season, is out again with a new soft-tissue injury and likely will target training camp for his return.</p><p>It’s clearly a group that needs stability, and Johnson can provide it. He’s been a non-concern for most of his run with the Bears. Stick him on Justin Jefferson or whoever else comes to town, and that’s pretty much a solved problem.</p><p>According to Pro Football Reference’s charting, the opposing quarterback has thrown at Johnson five or fewer times in 55 of his 77 career games. He has allowed three or fewer completions in 56 games.</p><p>If Johnson resumes playing like that, it’ll create margin for the Bears to figure out the other two spots and weather injuries. It’ll also go a long way for a defense that’s resetting at safety with free agent Coby Bryant and first-round pick <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/04/24/dillon-thieneman-got-to-the-nfl-by-using-criticism-to-improve-thatll-serve-him-well-with-the-bears" >Dillon Thieneman</a>. And for Johnson, it could earn him the additional long-term security he’s seeking.</p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" entries.summary: <h3>Theater</h3><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-3cf6be10-636b-11f1-a4c6-4556b34e5152"><li>One doesn’t see many Stephen Sondheim musicals at the Marriott Theatre, but now fans are in for a treat with one of the master’s best. Written with Hugh Wheeler, the Tony Award-winning musical <b>“A Little Night Music”</b> explores the complexities of love, longing and second chances revolving around actress Desirée Armfeldt (Alexandra Silber) and the men who love her. Nick Bowling directs. From June 17-Aug. 9 at Marriott Theatre, 10 Marriott Dr., Lincolnshire. Tickets: $80-$93. Visit <a class="Link" href="http://marriotttheatre.com" target="_blank" ><u>marriotttheatre.com</u></a>.</li><li><b>“Deserted”</b> is Melanie Coffey’s drama about a former city couple now living in rural America who attempt to grow a garden but find that farming provides more challenges than anticipated. Laura Sturm directs. From June 14-Aug. 2 at Redtwist Theatre, 1044 W. Bryn Mawr Ave. Tickets: $10-$60. Visit <a class="Link" href="http://redtwisttheatre.org" target="_blank" ><u>redtwisttheatre.org</u></a>.</li><li>Tin Drum Theatre presents <b>“Southern Rapture,”</b> Eric Coble’s drama, based on actual events, about a theater company in the Bible Belt and its decision to stage a play that sends the city into a frenzy. Jason Palmer directs. From June 11-28 at Theater Wit, 1229 W. Belmont Ave. Tickets: $30. Visit <a class="Link" href="http://tindrumtheatre.com" target="_blank" ><u>tindrumtheatre.com</u></a>.</li><li>BrightSide Theatre stages Mel Brooks and Thomas Meehan’s <b>“The Producers,”</b> a musical adaptation of the classic film about a pair of hapless producers on a mission to stage the biggest flop in theater history. Jeffrey Cass directs. From June 12-28 at Meiley-Swallow Hall, North Central College, 31 S. Ellsworth St. Tickets: $37. Visit <a class="Link" href="http://brightsidetheatre.com" target="_blank" ><u>brightsidetheatre.com</u></a>.</li><li>Paramount Theatre presents The Second City’s <b>“Laughing for All the Wrong Reasons,” </b>which features classic sketch comedy and songs plus new favorites. To June 20 at Copley Theatre, 8 E. Galena Blvd., Aurora. Tickets: $46. Visit <a class="Link" href="http://paramountaurora.com" target="_blank" ><u>paramountaurora.com</u></a>.</li><li>The 2026 <b>Opera Festival of Chicago</b> kicks off with its leading artists in concert (7:30 p.m. June 13 at Jarvis Opera Hall, DePaul University, 800 W. Belden Ave.) followed by performances of Giacomo Puccini’s “La Bohème” (7:30 p.m. June 26, July 1 and 2 p.m. July 5) and Francesco Cilea’s “Adriana Lecouvreur” (2 p.m. June 28 and 7:30 p.m. July 3). Both operas are performed at North Shore Center for the Performing Arts in Skokie, 9501 Skokie Blvd., Skokie. Tickets: $25-$91. Visit <a class="Link" href="http://operafestivalchicago.org" target="_blank" ><u>operafestivalchicago.org</u></a>.</li></ul><h3>Dance</h3><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: Affordable Care Act enrollment in Illinois continues to drop, new state data shows
entries.summary: <p>More than 92,000 people are no longer getting Affordable Care Act health insurance in Illinois, including a majority who were dropped because they didn’t pay their monthly premiums, according to new state data.</p><p>This lowers the number of people buying health insurance through the state’s marketplace exchange, Get Covered Illinois, than initially thought — driven by people who likely couldn't afford their plan. Overall, enrollment now stands at 373,065, which includes those who signed up after open enrollment closed for most people. This is a nearly 15% drop from the state’s record high of 437,892 in February 2025, according to data from KFF, which conducts health policy research and polling.</p><p>About 64% — or about 59,000 people — were disenrolled from their health insurance plan as of May 31 this year because of nonpayment, according to the state data. This year saw a higher percentage of people disenrolled for nonpayment since at least 2020, according to the state.</p><p>Another 28% of enrollees dropped coverage because they gained insurance another way or moved out of state.</p><p>In a statement, Get Covered Illinois said the increased costs in insurance led to one of the largest marketplace enrollment declines in nearly a decade because of federal policies.</p><p>“Federal policies implemented by the Trump Administration and Congressional Republicans have left Illinoisans facing unprecedented rising health care costs,” the statement read. “... As a state-based marketplace, Get Covered Illinois was able to blunt some of the decline through premium alignment strategies and public outreach and enrollment assistance, but the Trump Administration's federal actions will continue to impact our residents’ access to affordable health care coverage.”</p><p>The enrollment decrease in Illinois for nonpayment mirrors national figures. Earlier this year, the Wall Street Journal reported that about one in seven people across the country didn’t pay their premiums through the Affordable Care Act.</p><p>Advocates say this is what they feared would happen when Congress last year did not extend enhanced tax credits that dated back to the COVID-19 pandemic. Those enhanced tax credits had made health insurance through the exchange more affordable, according to Kathy Waligora, a leader with the Protect Our Care Illinois. The tax credits were at the center of last fall’s historic government shutdown, though lawmakers never were able to gain enough support to extend them.</p><p>“It was really exactly what we expected, and really concerning to see the scale,” Waligora said. “I think probably the most disappointing part is people wanted to be insured or they allowed themselves to be autorenewed and they couldn’t remain insured because of the cost of premiums.”</p><p>The state’s data shows that even with the expiration of those tax credits, about 85% of enrollees continue receiving some other form of financial assistance. Still, most of those dropped from their health care plan have annual incomes ranging from $23,475 to $48,225, according to state data.</p><p>Obamacare monthly premiums in Illinois rose by 25% this year, but that's still not as much as expected. State officials had originally predicted enrollees would see an average increase of 78%.</p><p>Waligora credited the state with trying to mitigate changes to the Affordable Care Act by, for example, extending the open enrollment period and trying to provide more information about different types of healthcare plans. Still, she described the lower enrollment numbers as a “shocking change” reflecting broader affordability issues in health care.</p><p>“We ignore this really loud signal we’ve gotten with the number of people disenrolling, likely going uninsured, because the marketplace coverage is unaffordable, if we don’t act on that, it’s going to have this ripple effect in the system,” Waligora said.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/04/24/obamacare-health-insurance-illinois-aca-tax-subsidies" >Obamacare premiums in Illinois rose sharply but not as much as expected</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: City panel approves Greyhound station purchase
entries.summary: <p>A City Council committee on Wednesday approved the purchase of the endangered Greyhound bus station, setting the stage for a full Council vote to create Chicago's first publicly owned intercity bus terminal.</p><p>Wednesday's vote to endorse buying the South Loop property for $19 million further reduces the chance of Greyhound's eviction, which would <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2024/08/27/greyhound-station-flixbus-bus-intercity" target="_blank" >kick thousands passengers, many of them low-income, to the curb</a>.</p><p>The move also raises the possibility of a multi-million dollar investment to improve the neglected terminal at 630 W. Harrison St.</p><p>"I worry about the continued degradation of this station if we continue to do nothing," Ald. Bill Conway, whose 34th Ward encompasses the station, told members of the Committee on Housing and Real Estate before the vote.</p><p>Conway has hesitated to keep the station at its current location. The terminal has been a hotspot for crime, including the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2022/10/24/23421080/person-fatally-shot-fatally-greyhound-station-near-west-side" target="_blank" >2022 murder of a Greyhound employee</a>. But on Wednesday Conway said the city could not underestimate the need for an intercity bus terminal, especially one that, for now, is owned by a private investment firm that previously stated it wanted to build a high-rise at the site.</p><p>"The alternative of doing nothing is a disastrous one for the people of Chicago," Conway said.</p><p>The sale to the city could close in August if the <a class="Link" href="https://occprodstoragev1.blob.core.usgovcloudapi.net/matterattachmentspublic/c7506480-9325-49c7-b02c-4698287c4bf4.pdf" target="_blank" >ordinance</a> is approved by the Council, Julie Hernandez-Tomlin, commissioner of the Department of Fleet and Facility Management, told the committee.</p><p>Greyhound would continue operating the station for one year after the sale date while the city finds a third-party to operate and maintain it, she said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a Harrison St., shown in 2023. It opened in 1989 to replace an aging, run-down station on Randolph Street in the Loop. Its modern design uses white cables suspended from blue masts to support the roof. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Bus operators would pay rent to use the station, not unlike how the city runs O'Hare and Midway airports, with those funds expected to cover operating expenses, she said.</p><p>Nearly 500,000 people used the Greyhound station last year, she said.</p><p>The city would begin almost immediately to improve the terminal, built in 1989. Crews would upgrade the heating and air conditioning system by the end of 2027, and security features such as cameras and lightening would be improved, Hernandez-Tomlin said. </p><p>After that, the city would identify other potential upgrades, such as accessibility compliance and updated restrooms.</p><p>Four members of the 20-person committee voted against the ordinance.</p><p>Ald Marty Quinn (13th), called the purchase "not a good deal," a "colossal risk," and a potentially poor use of $50 million of tax increment financing district money — something the city may regret when facing a billion-dollar budget gap later this year, he added.</p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson's office introduced the ordinance to authorize the purchase of the station from its current owner, Twenty Lakes Holdings, a real estate division of Alden Global Capital, which acquired the property during a sell-off of Greyhound stations in 2022.</p><p>The Greyhound terminal came to the brink of eviction in 2024 as its lease was set to expire — but was saved by a last-minute offer of a month-to-month extension.</p><p>The new owner had planned to raze the terminal and build a high-rise, but later backed out of those plans and entered negotiations to sell it to the city.</p><p>The product of those negotiations became public last year when a $50-million line item to buy the terminal was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/11/04/bill-conway-mayor-brandon-johnson-plan-greyhound-station-tif-funds" target="_blank" >discovered</a> in Johnson's proposed budget.</p><p>A year earlier, Johnson's former chief operating officer, John Roberson, had <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2024/08/08/greyhound-bus-union-station-flixbus" target="_blank" >said buying the terminal was unfeasible</a> due to the costs needed to renovate the poorly maintained building. But the city now says finding another location and building a new terminal would be even more expensive.</p><p>In February, a city committee <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/02/05/greyhound-station-mayor-johnson-intercity-bus-terminal" target="_blank" >moved to expand</a> the Canal/Congress tax increment financing district to include the Greyhound station, allowing for the potential future purchase.</p><p></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2023/4/29/23691124/greyhound-terminal-harrison-street-sale-intercity-bus-travel-depaul-university-study-lee-bey-column" target="_blank" >Lee Bey: Intercity bus terminals used to be a big part of big-city downtowns</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
